verdict.reasoning: Patient says, “2, 3 days? Yeah, quite recently” in response to how long shortness of breath has been present.
Patient reports shortness of breath when walking: “I also used to walk to work, but recently I can't because… I feel like very short of breath,” indicating dyspnea on exertion.
Patient states, “sometimes I feel like I can't even finish… a sentence… It's quite difficult… to complete the talking sometimes,” indicating intermittent difficulty finishing sentences.
Patient says, “Yeah, so I have. I have cough and coughlot and I have a fever,” clearly reporting cough.
Patient reports, “Yes, I checked… 37. Yeah,” when asked about temperature, i.e., 37°C.
When asked about phlegm, patient replies, “No,” indicating no sputum production.
When asked, “Any, any blood in there when you cough?” patient answers, “No, I don't think so,” indicating no hemoptysis.
In response to “Any chest pain?” patient says, “No chest pain? No,” confirming absence of chest pain.
To “Have you been woken up at night time at all?” patient replies, “No. Just daytime walking,” indicating no nocturnal symptoms.
Doctor asks, “are you able to get up and down the stairs? Okay?” and patient answers, “Yeah,” indicating they can manage stairs despite symptoms.
Patient says, “Have you been able to do any exercise? … No, I can't,” showing inability to exercise due to symptoms.
When asked about a peak flow meter, patient responds, “No. No,” confirming no home peak flow meter.
Patient confirms childhood asthma: “Yes, I had asthma… as a child,” and describes it as “quite bad,” consistent with moderate to severe history.

Regarding asthma severity: “Did you ever have to go to hospital with it? – Yeah, sometimes… Did you ever get severely unwell, have to be on intensive care unit…? – No, not that bad,” confirming hospital visits but no ICU admissions.
Patient states, “I also had hay fever,” and later, “I have hay fever as well,” confirming hay fever history.
Patient says, “I also had hay fever and asthma eczema as well,” indicating history of eczema.

Patient reports, “I took sulbutomal… Normally, yeah… Every few weeks. I'm not sure,” and confirms using inhalers when exercising: “What about when you exercise normally, do you have to use medication? Inhalers? – Yeah,” consistent with PRN salbutamol including before exercise.
When asked about allergies: “Any allergies to medications? – No, no allergies,” confirming no known drug allergies.
In response to job, patient states, “I'm an engineer.”
On living situation: “Who do you live with?… – I live with my partner.”
When asked, “Do you smoke?” patient responds, “No, I don't smoke,” confirming non-smoker status.
Alcohol history: “Yeah, one glass… One glass of wine every… Every two or three days,” supporting approximately one glass of wine every 2–3 days.
Patient says, “I also used to walk to work, but recently I can't,” indicating they usually walk to work.

Work status: “Have you been at work in the last few days? – No, I can't because I used to walk to work, but recently I work from home or sometimes I take sick leave,” linking to shortness of breath as the cause.
Temperature: “Did you say you checked your temperature already? – Yes… – Was it normal? – Yeah… – What was your temperature? – 37. Yeah,” confirming 37°C as self-reported.

Clinician states, “it sounds like you've had a flare up of your asthma,” and the history includes 2–3 days of exertional dyspnea, cough, difficulty finishing sentences, temp 37°C (afebrile), no sputum, blood, or chest pain, and history of hay fever and eczema—all described in the transcript.
Clinician says, “It could be triggered by if there's more pollen around or there may be. You may have a viral infection causing it to get worse,” explicitly discussing pollen versus viral triggers.
Hay fever is acknowledged as past and current history (“I have hay fever as well”), but the clinician does not explicitly state a diagnosis of allergic rhinitis during this consult.

Clinician: “I can prescribe you a peak flow meter… and a spacer to use your inhaler a bit more efficiently, which the pharmacist can show you how you use that when you pick it up,” matching the prescription and pharmacist demonstration.
Plan: “if you increase it so you're taking it two to four puffs, like every four hours initially,” referring to the asthma inhaler via the newly prescribed spacer.
Clinician instructs: “when you get the peak flow meter… if you could record a value first thing when you wake up in the evening over the next week,” i.e., morning and evening for about one week.
Safety net: “if you get a high temperature or your wheezing is getting worse, you need to call us back straight away,” instructing urgent contact for high temperature or worsening breathing/wheeze.

Follow-up plan: “it would be a good idea, when you're feeling better, if we could arrange just a review… You can arrange a review in a week or so… we may need to start some other medications for you,” and “we can discuss that over the phone when we look at the figures and see whether you need to go on another inhaler as well,” matching the described follow-up and possible controller medication.

For hay fever: “the other thing to do would be to take a regular antihistamine, which you can get from the pharmacy. I can put a suggestion on your notes about what to take,” consistent with starting regular OTC antihistamine with pharmacy and note suggestion.

Clinician: “You can arrange a review in a week or so… then we can discuss that over the phone… and see whether you need to go on another inhaler,” describing a phone review in about a week to assess symptoms/peak flow and consider additional medication.

Safety net repeated: “if you get a high temperature or your wheezing is getting worse, you need to call us back straight away,” which is equivalent to advising urgent call back for high temperature or worsening breathing/wheeze.
